tasks.prompt: Order the steps for deciding whether to decommission an aging storage facility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a decision on a small elevated tank at the end of its coating and structural life.

cards.label: Confirm the storage, fire and turnover role the facility plays in its zone today
Model zone operation without the facility under peak, fire and outage conditions
Compare rehabilitation cost with replacement and with the cost of operating without it
Consult operations, fire services and affected customers on the options and risks
Decide and record the option chosen with the conditions that must be met first
If decommissioning is chosen, plan isolation, draining, disinfection of affected mains and site restoration

tasks.explanation: The decision starts with what the tank actually does today, not what it was built for. Modelling without it exposes hidden roles before money is compared, and conditions are recorded so decommissioning cannot proceed until its replacements are real.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for completing the distribution asset registry to a trustworthy standard.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: mains, valves, hydrants, services and meters across the whole system.

cards.label: Define the asset classes, attributes and condition fields the registry must carry
Reconcile the registry against construction records, maps and field counts by area
Field verify a sample of records in each area and measure the error rate found
Correct the systematic errors the sampling reveals, such as missing valve records in older areas
Set a rule that no project closes until its as built asset records are loaded
Report registry completeness by asset class to management every year

tasks.explanation: Standards come before cleanup so staff know what complete means. Sample verification measures the true error rate instead of assuming it, and the project close rule stops new gaps forming while old ones are fixed.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the condition assessment strategy for distribution assets.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: assessment methods for mains, valves, hydrants, storage and pumping assets.

cards.label: Group assets by class and by how their condition can realistically be observed
Select the assessment method for each group, from break and leak history to direct inspection
Set the assessment cycle for each group based on failure consequence
Pilot the methods on one asset group and check the data is usable for renewal decisions
Roll the program out and load results into the asset registry as they are completed
Review whether condition data changed any renewal decision each year and adjust the methods

tasks.explanation: Methods must match how an asset can actually be observed, buried mains are judged by history and testing, not visual grades. Piloting proves the data can drive decisions, and the annual check asks the hard question of whether the program changed anything.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for prioritizing main renewal using risk based ranking.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual renewal candidate list for water mains across all districts.

cards.label: Score each candidate main for likelihood of failure from age, material, break and leak history
Score each candidate for consequence of failure from customers, critical services, flooding and repair cost
Combine the scores into a risk ranking and review the top candidates with operations staff
Check the top candidates against planned road and development work for coordination savings
Select the renewal program that fits the budget from the top of the coordinated list
Record why any high risk main was deferred and what monitoring applies until it is renewed

tasks.explanation: Likelihood without consequence renews quiet streets while a hospital feed waits. Operations review catches data errors the scores miss, road coordination stretches the budget, and deferrals are recorded with monitoring rather than forgotten.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the ten year distribution capital plan.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: renewal, growth, storage, pumping and program capital for ten years.

cards.label: Collect project needs from asset risk, capacity strategies, growth forecasts and regulatory duties
Scope and cost each project at a planning level with its driver and required year
Smooth the annual totals so delivery capacity and funding are realistic in each year
Identify the projects that cannot be deferred without breaching a standard or a duty
Present the plan with funding sources and the risks of the deferred projects stated
Update the plan annually, moving completed work out and new evidence in

tasks.explanation: Needs arrive from four different drivers and must compete in one list. Smoothing prevents a fantasy plan with three major projects in one year, non deferrable duties are identified plainly, and annual updates keep the plan a tool rather than a monument.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the valve and hydrant lifecycle program at system scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: exercising, inspection, repair and replacement cycles for all valves and hydrants.

cards.label: Confirm the inventory counts and the current exercising and inspection completion rates
Set cycle targets by criticality, with isolation valves on critical feeds exercised most often
Build the annual work plan by area so crews complete whole districts rather than scattered sites
Require found defects to generate a repair work order with a priority and due date
Track operability rates, not just visits completed, as the program measure
Report the percentage of critical valves proven operable to management each year

tasks.explanation: Completion rates can look healthy while critical valves still fail, so the program measures operability. Criticality sets the cycles, district based work cuts travel waste, and defects become dated work orders instead of notes.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing delivery of a major distribution capital project.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: governance for a multi million dollar trunk main and storage project.

cards.label: Approve the project charter with scope, budget, schedule and the benefits it must deliver
Set decision gates where design, procurement and construction readiness are reviewed before proceeding
Require monthly reporting on cost, schedule, risk and scope changes against the charter
Control changes through a documented approval that states cost and service impact before work proceeds
Commission the works with pressure, disinfection and sampling acceptance before service
Close the project with a benefits review comparing delivered performance with the charter

tasks.explanation: A charter and gates stop a project drifting from its approved purpose one small change at a time. Change control prices decisions before they are built, and the closing benefits review holds the original case to account.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for establishing levels of service for distribution assets.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: customer and technical service levels for pressure, outages, quality and response.

cards.label: Describe the services customers receive in plain language, from pressure to outage notice
Set measurable levels for each service using current performance as the starting evidence
Cost the asset and operating effort needed to hold each proposed level
Consult management and council on the levels and their costs as a package
Adopt the levels and link them to the asset plan and the operating budget
Measure and publish performance against the adopted levels each year

tasks.explanation: Service levels written only by engineers miss what customers actually experience. Costing each level before adoption prevents promising a standard the budget cannot hold, and published measurement keeps the promise visible.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for updating the distribution asset management plan under Ontario asset planning requirements.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a plan update covering inventory, condition, service levels, lifecycle and funding.

cards.label: Update the inventory and condition summaries from the current asset registry
Report current performance against the adopted levels of service
Forecast lifecycle needs and costs for renewal, growth and operations over the plan period
Test funding scenarios and state the service risk in any scenario that underfunds renewal
Present the plan for council adoption with the funding recommendation
Set the annual measures that will show whether the plan is being followed

tasks.explanation: The plan is built from the live registry, not from the last plan edited forward. Funding scenarios must state their service risk honestly, and adoption is followed by annual measures so the plan governs real budgets.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for developing a funding strategy for the main renewal program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: rate, reserve and debt options for a growing renewal requirement.

cards.label: Forecast the renewal spending required over twenty years from the asset risk analysis
Model the current reserve balance and rate revenue against that requirement
Show the year reserves are exhausted and breaks rise if funding stays unchanged
Develop funding options mixing rate increases, reserve targets and debt for large projects
Recommend the option that keeps renewal ahead of deterioration at a stable rate path
Review the strategy at each capital plan update against actual break and cost trends

tasks.explanation: The twenty year forecast makes the cost of delay visible while it is still cheap to act. Options are judged on keeping renewal ahead of deterioration, not on the lowest increase this year, and the strategy is retested against real trends.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for launching a trenchless rehabilitation program for aging mains.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: lining and bursting candidates among structurally sound but deteriorated mains.

cards.label: Identify candidate mains where the pipe is structurally suitable and excavation is costly or disruptive
Confirm condition and host pipe suitability by inspection for the first candidate group
Select the rehabilitation method for each candidate based on capacity, services and condition
Pilot the program on one street group and measure cost, disruption and water quality results
Set the design, disinfection and sampling standard for rehabilitated mains from the pilot lessons
Program the proven candidates into the capital plan in priority order

tasks.explanation: Not every old main is a lining candidate, so suitability inspection gates the list. A pilot proves cost and water quality practice before the method is programmed at scale, and rehabilitated mains meet the same acceptance standard as new mains.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing a Drinking Water Quality Management Standard management review for distribution.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the annual management review covering all required inputs for the distribution system.

cards.label: Compile the required inputs, including audit results, incidents, water quality trends and infrastructure review
Summarize corrective actions from the year and which remain open past their due dates
Prepare the operational plan changes proposed from the year evidence
Circulate the input package to the review participants before the meeting
Hold the review with the owner representative, top management and the overall responsible operator
Record the decisions, actions, owners and due dates as the formal review outputs

tasks.explanation: Management review fails when inputs are assembled in the meeting instead of before it. Open corrective actions are stated plainly, participants receive the package in advance, and outputs are recorded as owned, dated actions.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for revising and endorsing the operational plan after management review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: operational plan revision covering procedures, risk assessment and program documents.

cards.label: List every change directed by the management review and by incidents during the year
Draft the revised sections with the staff who operate under them
Check the revisions against the standard elements so no required element is weakened
Obtain endorsement of the revised plan by the owner and top management as required
Issue the controlled revision and withdraw superseded copies from all points of use
Brief all affected staff on what changed and record the briefing in training records

tasks.explanation: Changes are drafted with the operators who live under them, which keeps procedures workable. Endorsement and controlled issue protect against the classic failure of three plan versions in three offices, and briefings are recorded as training evidence.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing the distribution risk assessment under the quality management standard.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: hazards and hazardous events from entry points to customer taps.

cards.label: List the current hazards and control measures for each distribution activity and facility
Review incidents, adverse results and near misses from the year for hazards the assessment missed
Re score risks where new evidence changes likelihood or consequence
Identify hazards whose control measures depend on one person or one unverified step
Add or strengthen control measures and assign owners for the changes
Record the reviewed assessment as a controlled document and brief supervisors on the changes

tasks.explanation: The year incidents are the test of the assessment, any hazard that actually occurred but was not listed proves a gap. Single person controls are treated as weak controls, and the reviewed assessment is controlled and briefed, not filed silently.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing operator competency under the quality management standard.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: competency for sampling, disinfection, repair, valve operation and emergency duties.

cards.label: List the essential duties and the competency each one requires
Compare each operator record against the duties they are assigned to perform
Identify duties where only one operator is competent and no backup exists
Build training and supervised practice plans to close the gaps and create backups
Verify competency by observed performance for the highest risk duties, not attendance alone
Report the competency position and the remaining gaps at management review

tasks.explanation: A certificate alone does not prove competency for a specific duty, so records are compared duty by duty. Single operator duties are the real risk, and observed performance verifies the duties where an error hurts the public.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing the infrastructure maintenance program at management review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: planned maintenance for storage, pumping, valves, hydrants and mains programs.

cards.label: Compile planned maintenance completion and backlog for every program area
Identify overdue work on critical assets and the risk it has been carrying
Review whether unplanned repair work is crowding out planned maintenance
Rebalance crew and contractor resources toward the critical backlog
Set the completion targets and reporting for the next year
Record the review decisions in the management review outputs with owners and dates

tasks.explanation: Completion percentages hide risk unless the overdue critical work is named separately. The review confronts whether emergency work is eating the planned program, and rebalancing is recorded as a management decision with targets.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing the sampling and monitoring program under the quality management standard.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: regulatory sampling, operational checks and continuous monitoring in distribution.

cards.label: Compare the completed sampling against the regulatory schedule and the operational plan commitments
Review any missed, late or rejected samples and the causes recorded for them
Check continuous monitor and field instrument records for gaps and drift
Confirm the program changes needed for new sites, new parameters or past failures
Update the sampling procedures and the annual calendar with the agreed changes
Report the review outcome as an input to management review

tasks.explanation: The review compares what was done with what was promised in the plan and the regulation, not just with last year. Causes of missed samples are examined so the fix addresses scheduling or staffing, and changes flow into procedures and the calendar.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for strengthening the calibration program for distribution measurement devices.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: chlorine analysers, pressure recorders, flow meters and field test kits.

cards.label: Inventory every device used for operational decisions or regulatory records with its calibration interval
Review calibration records for overdue devices and for devices repeatedly found out of tolerance
Remove or tag out any device overdue for calibration that supports a regulatory record
Schedule calibrations so no week loses all devices of one type at once
Set the acceptance limits and the action taken when a device fails calibration
Audit the program quarterly and report overdue devices to the overall responsible operator

tasks.explanation: An inventory with intervals is the foundation, devices cannot be calibrated on a schedule nobody wrote. Overdue devices supporting regulatory records are removed at once, and repeat failures trigger replacement decisions rather than endless adjustment.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for running the internal audit program for the distribution quality management system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: internal audits of operational plan elements across facilities and programs.

cards.label: Build the audit schedule so every element and facility is audited within the cycle
Assign auditors who are independent of the area they will audit
Brief auditors on the criteria, evidence sampling and nonconformance grading
Conduct the audits and record findings against specific plan requirements
Issue findings to the responsible supervisors with response due dates
Verify closure of corrective actions at the next audit and report the program at management review

tasks.explanation: Independence is protected in assignment because self audits find little. Findings cite the specific requirement so responses can be precise, and closure is verified at the next audit rather than accepted on a promise.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for tracking corrective actions from audits, inspections and incidents to closure.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one corrective action register for quality management, ministry inspection and incident findings.

cards.label: Enter every finding into one register with its source, owner and risk based due date
Require a root cause statement for significant findings before an action is accepted
Review the register monthly with supervisors and escalate overdue high risk actions
Verify completed actions by evidence, such as a record, photo or re inspection, before closing
Analyse closed actions yearly for repeating causes that need a system fix
Report the register status, including overdue items, at management review

tasks.explanation: One register stops findings living in separate inboxes until they are forgotten. Root cause is required for significant findings so actions fix systems, and closure needs evidence, because an action marked done is not the same as a problem fixed.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for communicating management review outputs to all distribution staff.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: decisions and actions from the annual management review affecting field operations.

cards.label: Summarize the review decisions in plain language, separating what changes for field staff
Brief supervisors first so they can answer crew questions consistently
Present the changes at crew meetings with the reasons drawn from the year evidence
Update the procedures, forms and training affected by the decisions
Set the dates by which each change takes effect and who confirms it is in place
Check at the next quarterly review that the changes are actually in use in the field

tasks.explanation: Staff hear decisions through supervisors first so the message is consistent, not rumour driven. Documents and training are updated to match, and a field check confirms the change is real practice rather than a memo.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for updating the distribution emergency response plan at utility scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plan update covering breaks, contamination, supply loss, power loss and extreme weather.

cards.label: Review every emergency and near miss from the past two years against the current plan
Update contact lists, mutual aid details and authority delegations and verify them by test calls
Revise the response procedures where events showed the plan was wrong or silent
Confirm the equipment, bottled water and contractor resources the plan assumes are actually available
Issue the revised plan to all response roles and collect the superseded copies
Exercise the revised plan within the year and record the lessons as the next update input

tasks.explanation: Events are the audit of an emergency plan, so the update starts from what actually happened. Assumed resources are verified physically, contacts are test called, and an exercise is scheduled because an untested revision is still a draft.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps during a major trunk main break affecting a whole zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a trunk main break with zone wide pressure loss and road flooding.

cards.label: Confirm the break location and scale from field reports and SCADA pressure and storage trends
Direct isolation of the break and the zone support measures, including interzone transfers
Declare the emergency level and assign incident roles for operations, communications and liaison
Notify the health unit, municipality and affected critical customers and issue public information
Approve the repair plan, the return to service disinfection and sampling requirements
Stand down the emergency only after pressure, residuals and samples confirm normal service, then order the incident review

tasks.explanation: Scale is confirmed from data and field reports before the emergency level is set. Isolation and zone support protect the rest of the system, roles and notifications run in parallel under clear leadership, and stand down waits for water quality evidence.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps for deciding and managing a boil water advisory for part of the system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a suspected contamination or pressure loss event affecting one area of the system.

cards.label: Gather the evidence, including pressure records, residuals, samples and the event cause, for the health unit
Consult the medical officer of health, who directs whether an advisory is issued
Define the advisory area precisely by streets and facilities and prepare the public notice
Issue the notice through municipal channels, direct outreach to critical and vulnerable customers
Direct the corrective actions and the resampling program the health unit requires
Lift the advisory only on the direction of the medical officer of health after satisfactory results, and notify the same audience

tasks.explanation: The advisory decision belongs to the medical officer of health, so leadership starts by putting complete evidence in front of that office quickly. The area is defined precisely, lifting follows the same authority and evidence standard as issuing, and notification reaches the same people both times.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps when the treatment supply to distribution is interrupted for many hours.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a planned or unplanned treatment outage with the system living on storage.

cards.label: Calculate the hours of storage available by zone at current and at reduced demand
Stop non essential distribution water use and suspend permits and planned flushing
Set zone refill and draw priorities so critical customers and fire storage are protected
Issue conservation messaging scaled to the calculated storage position
Coordinate restart with treatment so zones refill in the priority order without pressure shocks
Review residuals and pressures across the system after supply is restored and log the event fully

tasks.explanation: Storage arithmetic drives every decision, because hours available differ by zone. Demand is cut and priorities set before the public appeal, restart is coordinated to avoid creating a second incident, and quality is verified after the event, not assumed.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps after a suspected contamination entry into the distribution system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a suspected backflow or intrusion event reported at a commercial premises.

cards.label: Isolate the suspected area by closing the boundary valves identified in the cross connection records
Collect samples for the parameters indicated by the suspected contaminant, with health unit advice
Notify the health unit and the ministry as required and agree the public communication approach
Direct flushing or draining of the isolated area under controlled conditions
Hold the area out of normal service until results and the health unit clear its return
Complete the incident investigation, including the cross connection failure that allowed entry

tasks.explanation: Isolation comes before investigation because containing a contaminant outranks explaining it. Sampling follows the suspected contaminant with health unit advice, return to service needs clearance, and the investigation must reach the cross connection failure or the event can repeat.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the standby power strategy for booster and storage sites.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: generators and transfer equipment for all booster stations and critical storage sites.

cards.label: Rank sites by the consequence of a power loss, including zone size, storage cover and critical customers
Confirm the load each site generator must carry, including the largest pump and controls
Test generators under real load at the ranked sites and record any that fail to carry it
Set the fuel, maintenance and refuelling arrangements for an outage lasting several days
Place generator upgrades for the highest risk sites in the capital plan
Exercise a multi site outage scenario yearly and update the strategy from the results

tasks.explanation: Ranking by consequence decides where generator money matters. Load testing under real load is the only proof that counts, fuel arrangements are planned for days not hours, and the yearly exercise tests the strategy rather than the paperwork.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for activating a mutual aid agreement during a distribution emergency.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: requesting crews and equipment from a neighbouring utility under an existing agreement.

cards.label: Confirm the emergency need exceeds internal crew, equipment and contractor capacity
Contact the partner utility duty officer with the specific crews, skills and equipment required
Agree the scope, supervision, safety requirements and cost terms before resources travel
Brief arriving crews on local procedures, water quality requirements and the work assigned
Integrate mutual aid work into the incident records and the disinfection and sampling controls
Release the resources, reconcile costs and send the formal thank you and debrief notes

tasks.explanation: Mutual aid is requested for a defined gap, not as a general call for help. Terms and safety are agreed before travel, outside crews work under local water quality controls, and costs and thanks are closed properly so the agreement is healthy for the next event.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for designing and running a distribution emergency exercise.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a tabletop exercise on a contamination scenario for supervisors and partner agencies.

cards.label: Set the exercise objectives, such as notification speed and advisory decision quality
Build a realistic scenario with timed injects based on a real past event pattern
Invite the roles that would actually respond, including health unit and municipal communications staff
Run the exercise and record decisions, delays and information gaps as they occur
Debrief participants the same day and agree the corrective actions and owners
Track the actions to closure and test the weakest one again in the next exercise

tasks.explanation: Objectives decide what the exercise can prove, so they are set before the scenario is written. Real partner roles expose the handoff gaps internal exercises miss, and the weakest finding is deliberately retested next time.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the system for a prolonged extreme cold emergency.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: system wide preparation for a forecast week of extreme cold and rising break rates.

cards.label: Review break, frozen service and staffing lessons from the last extreme cold event
Pre position repair clamps, pumps and generators and confirm contractor standby arrangements
Set the extra staffing and standby roster for the forecast period, including supervisory coverage
Issue customer messaging on protecting household plumbing and reporting breaks
Raise storage targets slightly and defer non essential work that would isolate mains
Hold a daily coordination call during the event to reassign crews to the highest priority breaks

tasks.explanation: Preparation is driven by the last event lessons rather than a generic checklist. Materials, contractors and rosters are set before the breaks start, storage and work deferrals reduce risk, and daily coordination keeps crews on the breaks that matter most.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for completing a post incident review after a significant distribution emergency.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a formal review after any event that triggered the emergency plan.

cards.label: Reconstruct the event timeline from logs, SCADA, recordings and participant notes
Compare the response against the emergency plan and the regulatory duties that applied
Identify what worked, what failed and what succeeded only by individual effort
Agree corrective actions with owners and due dates, including plan and training changes
Present the review to senior management with the actions and any funding required
Verify the actions are complete at the stated dates and close the review formally

tasks.explanation: The timeline is rebuilt from records before opinions are heard, because memory edits itself. Successes that depended on one person are treated as system weaknesses, and actions are verified at their dates so the review changes the next response.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for benchmarking energy use across the pump fleet.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: energy per cubic metre delivered for every booster and transfer station.

cards.label: Compile energy use and pumped volumes for every station for the past twelve months
Calculate the energy intensity of each station in kilowatt hours per cubic metre
Adjust the comparison for the lift and pressure each station works against
Identify the stations whose intensity is well above comparable stations
Investigate the worst stations for worn pumps, throttling and control problems
Set the improvement targets and report the fleet benchmark to management annually

tasks.explanation: Raw energy totals mislead because stations lift water different heights, so intensity is adjusted for lift before stations are judged. The worst performers are investigated for physical causes, and the benchmark repeats annually so improvement is visible.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting a time of use pumping schedule strategy for the system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: shifting storage filling to off peak electricity periods across all stations.

cards.label: Analyse the electricity price periods and the demand pattern of each zone
Confirm the storage available to carry each zone through the peak price period
Set fill schedules that complete filling before the peak period without breaching turnover targets
Check fire storage and emergency reserve are never traded away for price savings
Implement the schedules in the control system and brief operators on the override rules
Compare energy cost per cubic metre monthly against the pre strategy baseline

tasks.explanation: Price periods and zone demand together show where shifting is possible. Storage cover and fire reserve are hard limits that savings cannot cross, overrides are defined for operators, and monthly comparison proves the strategy saves money rather than just moving numbers.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for running a pump efficiency testing program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: wire to water efficiency tests for the major pumps in the fleet.

cards.label: Select the test order by pump size, running hours and suspected efficiency loss
Measure flow, head and electrical input under controlled test conditions for each pump
Calculate wire to water efficiency and compare it with the original duty performance
Rank pumps by the annual energy cost of their efficiency loss
Decide repair, refurbishment or replacement for the worst pumps through the capital process
Retest after any major work and record the recovered efficiency in the asset history

tasks.explanation: Testing follows size and suspicion so the largest losses are found first. Efficiency is compared with the pump original duty, losses are priced per year to rank action, and retesting after work proves the money bought efficiency back.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for evaluating variable speed drive retrofits for booster stations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a retrofit evaluation for constant speed stations with wide demand swings.

cards.label: Profile the flow and pressure demand of the candidate station across a full year
Estimate the energy wasted by throttling or cycling at the low demand periods
Confirm the pumps, motors and electrical supply are suitable for drive operation
Compare retrofit cost with the energy and maintenance savings over the drive life
Pilot the retrofit at the station with the strongest case and measure the result
Decide the fleet rollout order from the pilot evidence and place it in the capital plan

tasks.explanation: A year of demand profile decides whether a drive helps, because drives save money only where demand varies. Suitability is confirmed before costing, a pilot measures real savings, and rollout order follows evidence rather than sales ranking.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for completing an energy audit of the booster station network.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: an audit covering pumping, controls, building systems and operating practice.

cards.label: Collect energy, flow, pressure and running hour data for every station for the audit period
Visit each station to record equipment condition, control settings and operating practice
Identify energy waste, such as simultaneous heating and cooling, throttled pumps and leaking air or water systems
Quantify each saving opportunity with its cost and simple payback
Present the audit with the opportunities ranked for management decision
Implement the approved measures and track the verified savings for one year

tasks.explanation: Data collection precedes site visits so auditors arrive knowing where the energy goes. Opportunities are quantified and ranked by payback, and savings are verified after implementation because estimated savings are a promise, not a result.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reducing peak demand charges at the largest pumping stations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: demand management for stations whose peaks set the monthly demand charge.

cards.label: Analyse the interval energy data to find when each station demand peak occurs
Identify which pumps and events combine to set the peak in each billing period
Set control limits and staggered start rules so large pumps do not start together
Use storage to ride through the short peaks where levels safely allow
Alert operators when demand approaches the limit with time to act
Review the demand charge monthly and adjust the limits as zone demand grows

tasks.explanation: Interval data shows the peak is usually a coincidence of starts, not a steady load. Staggering and storage attack that coincidence, operator alerts give time to act, and monthly review keeps limits matched to growing demand.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting energy performance targets for distribution pumping.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual energy targets by station and for the fleet, reported to management.

cards.label: Establish the baseline energy intensity for each station adjusted for lift and volume
Set a target intensity for each station based on its tested condition and planned work
Assign the operational and capital actions that must deliver each target
Report intensity monthly with weather and demand context so operators are judged fairly
Investigate any station missing its target for two consecutive months
Reset targets annually after efficiency work is verified by retesting

tasks.explanation: Targets are set per station from its own tested condition, not as one fleet percentage that punishes high lift stations. Monthly context keeps reporting fair, and targets reset only on verified improvement.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the business case to replace an inefficient pump set on energy grounds.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a replacement case for a pump set with proven high energy losses.

cards.label: Confirm the efficiency loss by a wire to water test and price the annual wasted energy
Scope the replacement option, including any electrical or control work it requires
Calculate the simple payback and the life cycle cost difference against keeping the old set
Add the non energy benefits, such as reliability and parts availability, with honest weighting
Present the case in the capital plan ranked against other energy projects
If approved, set the baseline test so the saving can be verified after replacement

tasks.explanation: The case rests on a measured loss priced per year, not on pump age alone. Life cycle costing prevents a cheap purchase with expensive running, and a baseline test fixed in advance lets the promised saving be audited.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adding energy monitoring to the supervisory control system for pumping.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: energy and efficiency displays for all major stations in the control system.

cards.label: Define the energy measures operators need, including intensity, cost to date and demand against limit
Confirm the meters and signals available at each station and fill the gaps in the plan
Build the displays with the operators who will use them on shift
Set the alarms for high intensity and approaching demand limits
Train all shifts on reading the displays and the actions each alarm requires
Review after three months whether the displays changed operating decisions and adjust them

tasks.explanation: Measures are defined by the decisions operators must make, not by what is easy to display. Alarms are tied to defined actions, training covers every shift, and the three month review asks whether information became behaviour.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the annual energy and emissions report for distribution operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one annual report on pumping energy, cost and associated emissions.

cards.label: Compile total energy use, cost and pumped volume by station for the reporting year
Calculate fleet energy intensity and compare it with the target and the prior years
Convert energy use to emissions using the current published grid factors
Explain the main movements, separating growth, weather and efficiency effects
State the funded energy projects for the next year and their expected effect
Present the report to management and file it with the utility sustainability records

tasks.explanation: Growth and weather are separated from efficiency so the report does not credit or blame operators for the weather. Published factors keep emissions honest, and next year projects are stated with expected effects so the report leads somewhere.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for updating the cross connection control program policy and bylaw support package.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a program policy update covering hazard classes, testable devices and enforcement.

cards.label: Review program results, incidents and premises data since the last policy update
Compare the policy with current standards and the practice of comparable Ontario municipalities
Draft the updated requirements by premises hazard class with legal review of the bylaw wording
Consult affected groups, including large water users and the plumbing trade, on the practical effects
Present the policy and bylaw amendments to council for adoption
Set the effective dates, notice letters and inspector guidance before enforcement begins

tasks.explanation: Program evidence shows which requirements failed in practice before wording is drafted. Legal review and trade consultation prevent an unenforceable or impractical bylaw, and enforcement starts only after notice and guidance are ready.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for prioritizing hazard surveys of industrial, commercial and institutional premises.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: survey scheduling for all non residential premises in the system.

cards.label: Build the premises inventory from business licences, water accounts and property data
Classify premises by likely hazard using business type, from high hazard processes to low hazard offices
Rank surveys so high hazard and never surveyed premises are visited first
Assign survey work to certified staff and set the monthly completion targets
Record survey results in the program database the day they are completed
Report survey coverage by hazard class to management every quarter

tasks.explanation: The inventory is built from multiple sources because any single list misses premises. Hazard classification drives the order so the most dangerous connections are found first, and coverage is reported by class, not just by total visits.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for improving backflow preventer test compliance across the system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual test compliance for all testable devices on record.

cards.label: Reconcile the device inventory against survey records and past test reports
Send test due notices with clear deadlines and approved tester information
Send a reminder before the deadline and a non compliance notice after it
Offer a compliance window with escalating follow up for premises that respond
Apply the enforcement steps in the bylaw for premises that still do not test, up to water service action as authorized
Report the compliance rate by hazard class and target the lowest classes next year

tasks.explanation: Compliance work starts with a clean inventory, because notices sent for devices that no longer exist destroy credibility. Notices escalate in defined steps, enforcement follows the bylaw rather than frustration, and reporting by hazard class shows whether the riskiest devices are the compliant ones.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for escalating enforcement at a high hazard premises that refuses program requirements.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one industrial premises refusing survey access and device installation.

cards.label: Document the hazard evidence and every contact and refusal in the premises file
Issue the formal order or notice required by the bylaw with a clear deadline and requirements
Notify the overall responsible operator and municipal legal support of the escalation
Offer a final meeting with the premises owner to agree a compliance path
Apply the bylaw consequences on the deadline if compliance is not achieved, as authorized
Keep the premises on a watch list with re inspection until compliance is proven stable

tasks.explanation: A documented file is the foundation, enforcement collapses without it. Formal notice and legal support precede consequences, a final meeting keeps the door open, and watch list status prevents a one time fix from lapsing quietly.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting staffing and certification requirements for the cross connection program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: inspector and program administration staffing for a growing premises inventory.

cards.label: Calculate the workload from premises counts, survey cycles and annual test volumes
Define the roles and the certification each role requires under the program standard
Compare current staffing and certification with the requirement and identify the gaps
Schedule certification training and supervised field experience for staff closing gaps
Set the supervision and file review practice for newly certified inspectors
Review workload and staffing yearly against premises growth and compliance results

tasks.explanation: Workload is calculated from the inventory and cycles, not guessed from last year budget. Certification gaps are closed with supervised experience, new inspectors are reviewed until proven, and yearly review keeps staffing matched to a growing program.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building a public and trade education strategy for cross connection control.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: education for homeowners, plumbers, testers and large water users.

cards.label: Identify the audiences whose behaviour creates or prevents backflow risk
Set the key message and the required action for each audience
Choose the channels each audience actually uses, from permit counters to trade associations
Produce the materials with the program requirements stated in plain language
Deliver the campaign alongside survey and test notice cycles so messages reinforce action
Measure the effect through survey findings, test compliance and inquiry volumes

tasks.explanation: Education is aimed at behaviour, each audience gets a message tied to the action it must take. Timing materials with notice cycles makes education practical rather than decorative, and compliance measures show whether it worked.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership steps after a backflow incident contaminates a building water system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a chemical backflow into a commercial building, reported by the occupant.

cards.label: Isolate the building service and the affected street section if the contaminant may have reached the main
Sample the building system and the nearby mains for the reported contaminant with health unit advice
Notify the health unit and agree who communicates with the occupants and the public
Direct flushing and clearance sampling of the affected plumbing and mains
Require correction and testing of the backflow protection at the premises before service normalizes
Complete the program investigation and add the premises type to the survey priority list if it was missed

tasks.explanation: Isolation protects the main while the building is investigated. Health unit coordination controls communication, clearance is proven by sampling, and the program investigation asks why the premises was not already protected, because the incident is also a program failure signal.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up program data reporting for cross connection control.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a database and reporting routine for premises, devices, tests and enforcement.

cards.label: Define the data fields for premises, hazards, devices, tests, surveys and enforcement actions
Clean and migrate the existing records, resolving duplicate premises and orphan devices
Set the entry standard so field staff record results the day work is done
Build the routine reports, including compliance by hazard class and overdue tests
Review the reports monthly with program staff and act on the oldest overdue items
Present the annual program summary to management with the risk picture by hazard class

tasks.explanation: Fields are defined before migration so the new system does not inherit old confusion. Same day entry keeps reports real, monthly review works the overdue list, and the annual summary presents risk by class rather than activity counts.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for integrating cross connection requirements into new development approvals.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: requirements for new industrial, commercial and multi residential developments.

cards.label: Agree the program requirements for each development type with planning and building staff
Add the requirements to the development review checklist and the servicing agreement wording
Review development drawings for the required devices and their testable installation
Inspect and witness the initial test of devices before occupancy or final acceptance
Load the new premises and devices into the program database at acceptance
Include the premises in the normal survey and test notice cycles from the first year

tasks.explanation: Requirements agreed at the approval stage cost the developer little and the utility nothing, while retrofits cost both. Drawing review and witnessed first tests catch untestable installations, and database entry at acceptance means new premises never start as program orphans.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for auditing the cross connection control program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a program audit covering bylaw use, records, field practice and outcomes.

cards.label: Set the audit criteria from the bylaw, the program policy and the operational plan
Sample premises files across hazard classes and check survey, device and test records
Field check a sample of premises to confirm records match the installed protection
Compare program outcomes, including compliance rates and incidents, with the program goals
Report the findings with corrective actions, owners and due dates
Verify the corrective actions at the next program review and report the status to management

tasks.explanation: File sampling across hazard classes tests whether the riskiest premises get the most rigour. Field checks catch the gap between records and reality, and corrective actions are verified, not just reported, at the next review.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for designating overall responsible operator coverage for the system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: coverage arrangements for vacations, training and unplanned absence of the overall responsible operator.

cards.label: Confirm the certification and experience requirements the designate must hold for this system class
Name the primary and secondary designates in writing with the periods each covers
Brief the designates on current incidents, regulatory commitments and decisions in progress
Notify supervisors, control room staff and the health unit contact of the designation and its dates
Require the designate to log decisions made in the role in the operating record
Review the coverage after each period and update the designation list with any lessons

tasks.explanation: Designation is written and communicated before it is needed, because an emergency is the wrong time to discover who is in charge. Briefing covers live commitments, decisions are logged in the role, and each coverage period improves the arrangement.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a supervisory review of operator logbooks and operating records.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a monthly review routine for station logs, repair records and sampling entries.

cards.label: Set the review schedule so every facility record set is reviewed each month
Check entries for completeness, unusual readings and actions recorded against alarms
Follow up any entry showing an exceedance, missed check or unexplained change with the operator
Sign and date the review so the record shows supervisory oversight occurred
Trend the recurring record problems and address them through coaching or procedure changes
Report the review completion and significant findings to the overall responsible operator

tasks.explanation: A set schedule prevents review becoming an inspection time scramble. Follow up connects records to real events, the signature evidences oversight, and trending turns repeated small errors into a training or procedure fix.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for conducting performance and coaching reviews with distribution supervisors.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual reviews for zone and program supervisors reporting to the utility manager.

cards.label: Gather each supervisor results on safety, quality, program delivery and team development
Ask each supervisor for their self assessment and their support needs before the meeting
Hold the review meeting, recognizing strengths and agreeing the gaps plainly
Set two or three development goals with the training or experience that supports each
Record the agreed goals and review dates in the personnel file
Check progress at mid year and adjust support where a goal is stalled

tasks.explanation: Results across safety, quality and delivery give the review substance beyond impressions. Self assessment first makes the meeting a discussion, goals are few and supported, and the mid year check keeps development from being an annual surprise.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting a shift handover standard across distribution operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: handover between shifts at control rooms, stations and field crews.

Set the handover format, combining a written log entry with a direct conversation for critical items
Require the incoming operator to confirm understanding of the critical items before the outgoing shift leaves
Audit handovers monthly by sampling logs and asking incoming operators what they received
Correct the format or coaching where audits find information being lost
Review the standard after any incident where handover played a part

tasks.explanation: The standard defines content before format, because a neat form can still omit the one critical isolation. Confirmation by the incoming operator closes the loop, audits test what was received rather than what was written, and incidents feed the standard.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the system for a ministry drinking water inspection.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: readiness for a scheduled inspection of the distribution system and its records.

cards.label: Review the last inspection report and confirm every past finding is closed with evidence
Run a self inspection of facilities, records and sampling using the ministry focus areas
Correct the deficiencies the self inspection finds and file the evidence of correction
Brief the staff who will host the inspection on their areas and the records they own
Ensure the overall responsible operator and key supervisors are available during the inspection window
Log every inspector request during the inspection and respond within the time agreed

tasks.explanation: Past findings are checked first because repeat findings damage credibility most. A genuine self inspection finds problems while they can still be fixed, hosting staff know their records, and requests during the inspection are logged and answered promptly.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the annual report and summary required for the drinking water system.

tasks.configuration: Scope: the annual report and summary report for a large municipal residential system.

Confirm the report content against the requirements of Ontario Regulation 170/03 for annual and summary reports
Draft the summary in plain language a council member and a resident can follow
Have the overall responsible operator and management review the drafts for accuracy
Present the summary to council and make the annual report available to the public as required
File the reports and record where and when they were made available

tasks.explanation: Content is compiled from records and checked against the regulation before drafting style is considered. Plain language serves the actual audience, senior review protects accuracy, and availability is documented because the duty includes making the report accessible, not just writing it.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building an operator training and certification progression plan.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: progression planning for all distribution operators over three years.

Identify the roles the system needs filled at each certificate level over the next three years
Match operators to progression paths and set target examination windows
Provide study support, course time and supervised experience toward each target
Track examination results and adjust the plan where an operator needs a second attempt
Report progression against the plan at management review each year

tasks.explanation: The plan matches individual progression to the roles the system will actually need, not to ambition alone. Study support and experience are scheduled as work, second attempts are planned without stigma, and management review keeps the pipeline visible.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting an escalation framework for operational decisions by supervisors.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: decision rights for breaks, advisories support, overtime, contractors and public statements.

cards.label: List the recurring operational decisions and the risk each one carries
Set the level that may decide each item, from operator to supervisor to overall responsible operator
Define the situations that must escalate at once, including adverse results and media contact
Publish the framework where shifts can reach it and brief every supervisor on its use
Review escalations monthly to see whether decisions sat at the right level
Adjust the framework where reviews show bottlenecks or decisions taken too low

tasks.explanation: Decision rights are set before the emergency, when judgement is calm. Mandatory escalations protect the public and the operator, the framework is reachable on shift, and monthly review tunes it from real cases rather than theory.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for rolling out a new operating procedure across all distribution crews.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large Ontario municipal drinking water distribution system operating under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard. The overall responsible operator holds Class 4 distribution certification.
tasks.configuration: Scope: a revised main disinfection and return to service procedure for all zones.

cards.label: Finalize the procedure with field input and confirm it matches the operational plan
Identify the crews, supervisors and records the change affects
Train all affected staff and verify understanding for the critical steps
Issue the controlled procedure and withdraw the old version from every point of use
Audit the first jobs done under the new procedure in each zone
Correct training or wording where audits find the procedure is not being followed as written

tasks.explanation: Field input before finalizing prevents a procedure crews quietly work around. Training and controlled issue happen together, first job audits in every zone catch local misunderstandings, and audit findings are treated as feedback on the procedure as well as the crews.

tasks.prompt: Utility leadership review, case 1: the Northgate district metered area in an Ontario system shows minimum night flow climbing for two months while billed use stays flat, and managers must decide where the loss strategy should focus.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario district metered area with boundary meters, night flow logging, step testing and acoustic logging available.

evidence.label: Minimum night flow in Northgate rose from 3 L/s to 7 L/s over two months with no new customers added.
Daytime demand and billed consumption in the area are unchanged over the same period.
Boundary valve checks confirm the district is tight, with no flow through any closed boundary valve.
Step testing isolates the rise to one subzone of Northgate, where night flow falls by 3.7 L/s when its feed is closed briefly.
Acoustic logging in that subzone finds a strong leak noise at one fitting, and repair drops area night flow back to 3.2 L/s.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A growing leak in the one subzone of Northgate, not customer use, explains the doubled night flow
Night shift industry in the area has doubled its water use
The district meter has drifted and now overreads at night
A boundary valve is passing water into the district from the next area

inference.explanation: Billed use and daytime demand are flat, and boundary valves are proven tight, so industry use and inflow do not fit. Step testing localizes the rise to one subzone and repair restores night flow, which a drifting meter cannot explain.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation and guides the strategy?

options.label: Adopt weekly night flow trending for all districts with a set investigation trigger, starting with step testing when a trigger is crossed
Recalibrate the district meter and close the loss file
Raise customer rates in the district to cover the extra water

nextClue.explanation: Weekly trending with a trigger verifies the repair holds and catches the next leak early, which is the strategy the step test evidence supports.

clueText.nc-a: Night flow in Northgate holds near 3 L/s for the next quarter under weekly trending, and the trigger process is adopted system wide.
clueText.nc-b: Repair of a physical leak restored the flow, so meter drift was not the cause.
clueText.nc-c: The water was leakage, not customer use, so billing customers for it does not fix the loss.
